The Basus War alone is enough to show this, even though it began at the end of the fifth century CE. As is well known, the immediate cause was the killing of Kulayb ibn Rabi‘a by Jassas ibn Murra al-Shaybani after Kulayb wounded the udder of a camel belonging to Jassas’s maternal uncle. The camel had been grazing on land that Kulayb had set aside as protected pasture, where he allowed only his own camels to graze. Jawad Ali, vol. 4, p. 355.↩︎
One of the su‘luk poets, Urwa ibn al-Ward, who died thirty years before the Hijra, expressed this meaning in his famous poem in r rhyme:↩︎

> May God curse the poor outlaw who, when night falls, > goes among the butchered bones, familiar with every slaughter place, > counting himself rich whenever, for one night, > he finds enough food from a fortunate friend. See *al-Asma‘iyyat*, ed. Shakir and Harun, Dar al-Ma‘arif, Egypt, 1964, p. 45. In this vivid image, the poor outlaw has nothing at night except bare bones to chew, and the greatest wealth he can imagine is finding enough food for one night from a friend whose livestock has prospered and survived loss.

The person meant here is al-Muttalib ibn Abd Manaf, father of Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet’s grandfather. The alliance began when Banu Bakr ibn Abd Manat ibn Kinana planned during al-Muttalib’s time to drive Quraysh out of the Sanctuary and fight them. They gathered their forces; Quraysh did the same and prepared for war. Al-Muttalib then formed an alliance between Quraysh and the Ahabish—Banu al-Harith ibn Abd Manaf ibn Kinana, Banu al-Hun ibn Khuzayma ibn Mudrika, and Banu al-Mustaliq ibn Khuza‘a. They met Banu Bakr and their allies in battle, and Quraysh and its allies won while Banu Bakr were defeated. See al-Baladhuri, Genealogies, vol. 1, pp. 75–76. There are many reports of such alliances in Arab works, including al-Aghani, vol. 14, p. 61; Abu al-Fida, vol. 1, p. 108; Collection of Arab Poets, pp. 288, 394; Mus‘ab al-Zubayri, Genealogy of Quraysh, ed. Lévi-Provençal, Cairo, 1953, p. 9; al-Iqd al-Farid, vol. 6, p. 9; Ibn al-Athir, vol. 1, p. 366; and others.↩︎

Interestingly, some markets in the Arabian Peninsula did not impose the tithe because they were not located in the territory of a “kingdom”—that is, the tribal chief there had not taken the title of king. The market of al-Shihr is one example. Merchants there did not pay a tithe but instead paid a protection fee to the dominant chief. See Jawad Ali, vol. 4, pp. 414–415, quoting al-Muhabbar, pp. 263–267.↩︎

A tribe is a smaller unit than an ashira. An ashira is a group of several tribes joined by a common ancestry or a particular alliance. Quraysh, for example, was an ashira made up of roughly ten branches, including Hashim and Umayya.↩︎

Khasasa means poverty. Alb means a gathering of people united by hostility toward another person or group; one says, “they are all one alb against me.” The Prophet is therefore saying to Adi: I think what keeps you from Islam is what you see of the poverty of the Muslim community at that time, and the large number of our enemies.↩︎

Commercial contacts brought many things into pre-Islamic society: craft skills, practical knowledge of agriculture and technical tools, a variety of ideas and beliefs, and many urban customs. Tribal leaders and major Qurayshi merchants also adopted valuable household goods. Through their trading journeys, tribal chiefs and leading Qurayshi caravan merchants learned about political events in the outside world and about the social problems facing neighboring peoples. These problems accompanied the decline caused by the two empires exhausting themselves in struggles over the Mediterranean lands and the main parts of the Arabian Peninsula, especially Yemen and the Hijaz.↩︎

Some Orientalists used stories about Qusayy—stories mixing fiction and fact in the accounts of Ibn al-Kalbi, Ibn Ishaq, and Ibn Jurayj—to argue that Qusayy was a legendary figure. See Jawad Ali, vol. 4, pp. 194–195. Whatever the truth of that claim, our argument does not depend on whether a person named Qusayy actually existed. It depends on a firmly established historical fact: at a certain point, the Qurayshi aristocracy succeeded in extending its control over Mecca and delegated one of its leaders—whether his name was Qusayy or not—to represent that control on its behalf. History confirms both the existence of that control and the historical consequences that followed from it.↩︎

The people of the Hijaz in the pre-Islamic period divided the year into twelve months. Four were called the sacred months—three consecutive months, Dhu al-Qa‘da, Dhu al-Hijja, and Muharram, and one separate month, Rajab—because they were considered holy and fighting, aggression, and violation of sacred protections were forbidden in them. Fighting and raiding were permitted during the other eight months. Jawad Ali, vol. 8, p. 373.↩︎
